newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Amaritel to focus on local phone service.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Amaritel to focus on local phone service.

text.p: Telefonos de Mexico (Telmex) finally has a local rival.
In contrast with most of new entrants to Mexico's telephone market, Amaritel SA plans to focus on local service instead of the lucrative long-distance market, company officials said Tuesday.

Amaritel, majority owned by Grupo Radio Centro, on Monday won approval from the government to provide both long-distance and local telephone service. It became the 11th telephone company to win a concession to take on Telmex, which lost its decades-old monopoly last year.
Other rivals, which include such heavyweight companies as AT&T and MCI Communications, are already fighting for a share of the country's $4.0 billion long-distance market.
While others focus on long-distance, there is room in Mexico for another local provider to help bring telephones to far-flung areas that are currently unserved, Amaritel executives said.
Mexico currently has only about 9.6 telephone lines per 100 people, while officials have said they want the number of installed lines to double by 2000.
"Our rivals are all competing for a slice of the cake. We want to expand the size of the cake itself," said German Carmona Garduno, the director general of Amaritel.
"We plan to also offer long-distance service, but our focus is the local market," he told reporters during a news conference in Mexico City.

Carmona said Amaritel was 49 percent owned by U.S. Global Telecommunications, a joint venture between four small U.S. companies: Concord Telephone Co., Alltel Information Services, Hargray Communications Group and Farmers Telephone Co.
Amaritel plans to build its own network but it will also hook up with Telmex's massive existing network.
It aims to begin offering service in Mexico City, Puebla and Veracruz by the end of the year and sign up some 500,000 clients within five years.

The venture will require an initial capital investment of $70 million and about $700 million in five years. Officials said the company would reinvest any proceeds from the project and rely heavily on supplier credit contracts. They would not comment on how Radio Centro plans to raise its share of the money.

Mexico opened its doors to telephone competition last year. In 1997, it began to allow companies to connect to Telmex's existing network -- a move that allows them to reach millions of ordinary phones without building parallel networks of their own.

Most companies have focused solely on long-distance because of low local rates in Mexico and the huge cost of laying down a local network. Many also want to wait until Mexico comes through on its pledge to auction off parts of the radio spectrum that could be used in local wireless service.

Ameritel officials said local service in Mexico has become profitable in recent years, as the introduction of competition forced Telmex to stop cross-subsidies -- using long-distance revenue to keep local rates artificially low.
Carmona added that the local market could grow faster than long-distance.
